sources.title: Dániel Balogh, ed.: Hunnic Peoples in Central and South Asia, Sources for their Origin and History
sources.note: ERC-supported multilingual sourcebook used for the overview and concise override: Yueban appears securely in Chinese history only in 437 to 448, and proposed links to Avars or Hephthalites remain competing theories.

sources.title: Wei Shu 102: Western Regions, Yueban passage
sources.note: Primary Classical Chinese text used for exact wording about origin, title, grooming, medicine, ritual claims, diplomacy and court adoption of Yueban music.

sources.title: Taiping Yulan 799: Yueban
sources.note: Later Chinese encyclopedic transmission of the Yueban notice, used for the parallel original wording about weather specialists, medicine, washing, and court adoption of drum-and-dance rhythms.

sources.title: Wei Shu, Wusun, Yueban and neighboring states: English translation
sources.note: Readable translation used alongside the Chinese original for location, population claim, hair treatment, bathing and sulfur; court ethnography is explicitly treated as external testimony.

sources.title: Chinese Text Project: Wei Shu bibliographic entry
sources.note: Text-history reference used to identify Wei Shou’s 554 compilation and the external Classical Chinese context of the written sample.

sources.title: Taishan Yu: A History of the Relationship Between the Chinese Dynasties and the Western Regions
sources.note: Detailed synthesis used for the Ili to Chu reconstruction, 437 and 448 embassies, Northern Wei response and explicit uncertainty around contacts and later fate.

sources.title: Armin Selbitschka: Tribute, Hostages, and Marriage Alliances in the Northern Wei Period
sources.note: Peer-reviewed diplomatic study used for the north-of-Issyk-Kul placement and the political purpose and military result of the 448 tribute-backed alliance request.

sources.title: Nikolay N. Kradin: From Tribal Confederation to Empire, The Evolution of Rouran Society
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study used to keep Rouran history distinct: formation in 402, Ili to Tarim reach, military organization and mid-fifth-century crisis.

sources.title: UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia II: The Nomads of Northern Central Asia
sources.note: Older scholarly synthesis used as a clearly labelled reconstruction of Yueban origins near Lake Balkhash, contrasted with the narrower secure chronology.

sources.title: UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia III: Northern Nomads
sources.note: Scholarly regional chapter used for its source-based summary of Tarbagatai placement, Northern Xiongnu ancestry, grooming and washing reports.

sources.title: Michael Frachetti and Alexei Mar’yashev: Long-Term Occupation and Seasonal Settlement at Begash
sources.note: Peer-reviewed regional archaeology used only as comparison: Phase 4 dates 70 to 550, intermittent habitation, hearths, trash pits, spindle whorls, iron work and spring-fed water.

sources.title: Robert Spengler III: Botanical Resource Use in the Central Eurasian Mountain/Steppe Interface
sources.note: Archaeobotanical dissertation used to confirm the 70 to 550 Begash phase, its conventional Wusun attribution and sparse productive remains; it is never relabelled Yueban.

sources.title: Dairy to millet synergy in the Inner Asian mountains from 2900 BCE
sources.note: Peer-reviewed biomolecular study used as explicitly regional food evidence for dairy, horse products, millet and increasing agrarian intake; it does not identify Yueban diners.

sources.title: An Imagined Past? Nomadic Narratives in Central Asian Archaeology
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis used to reject a uniform meat-only, always-moving stereotype and to frame mixed herding, farming and craft economies cautiously.

sources.title: Étienne de la Vaissière: Xiongnu, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly reference used to distinguish the earlier empire, Northern and Southern divisions, the post-153 evidence gap and uncertainty in language and continuity.

sources.title: Frantz Grenet: Kidarites, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly reference used to identify the Kidarites as a separate Tokharistan/Gandhara dynasty with their own coins and chronology.

sources.title: A. D. H. Bivar: Hephthalites, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly reference used to identify the Hephthalites as a distinct later political formation in Bactria, Iran and India.

sources.title: Alexander Savelyev and Choongwon Jeong: Early nomads of the Eastern Steppe
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed interdisciplinary study used for the weak evidentiary bridge between eastern steppe names and later western Huns or Avars.

proposedOverrides.summary: Secure records run 437 to 448; disappearance is undocumented, so 448 marks the last dated Yueban evidence, not extinction.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact imported id yueban is indexed circa 100 to 500, with four initial coverage intervals and no prior card or override.
It is absent at 1 BCE, present at 100, 200, 300 and 400, then absent at the indexed 500 endpoint and at 600.
All four exact snapshots are one-part, one-ring, nine-position Polygons with bounds [71.41931419314193, 44.50546215401255, 75.33615336153363, 47.772249836919286].

The 100, 200 and 300 raw coordinate hash is d5fce106a2f8d45ea140352a79c7db162273d47b573c146e5d47906126447ad2; 400 is b1d3e85fa37e2661e1bba78461e366f7b4aa5d1709acc90cbfe8e56357fc1766 only because its ring begins at another vertex.
All four rotation- and orientation-invariant canonical hashes equal c3bbdc5b2d998c0a00c5c47d341e5155b01198a4ba1cf343b45ac0161fe8f6bc.
The exact Yueban shape contains only the western Lake Balkhash test point and misses historical candidates in Ili, Chu, Tarbagatai, Issyk-Kul and north of Kucha.
Earlier Xiongnu and Southern Xiongnu and later Ruanruan remain separate atlas identities. No actual Xianbei, Kidarite or Hephthalite id exists in the audited index.
All coordinates, bounds, hashes and point tests describe imported display geometry only; none establishes ethnicity, language, migration, modern borders or exclusive sovereignty.
